value.overview: The Osprey is a distinctive fish-eating bird of prey found on every continent except Antarctica. It is strongly associated with water and can capture fish from both fresh and salt water. Long, narrow wings, a white head with a dark eye stripe, and powerful feet make it easy to recognize. Northern populations migrate seasonally, while some populations in warmer regions remain year-round. The species is the only living member of its family, Pandionidae.
value.classification: The Osprey is classified as Pandion haliaetus in the order Accipitriformes and family Pandionidae. It is sometimes called the Fish Hawk or Fish Eagle, although it is not a true eagle.
value.identification: A large, long-winged raptor, the Osprey measures about 55–63 cm in length and has a wingspan of roughly 1.5–1.8 m. Adults are dark brown above and white below, with a white head, dark eye stripe, yellow eyes, and a strongly hooked bill. In flight, the wings are narrow and often appear kinked at the wrists. Females commonly show more brown streaking across the upper breast than males. Juveniles have pale-edged feathers on the back.
value.rangeHabitat: The Osprey has a nearly worldwide distribution around suitable fish-bearing waters, including coastlines, estuaries, rivers, lakes, reservoirs, marshes, and mangroves. In Costa Rica it is a widespread migrant and winter visitor, occurring along both Pacific and Caribbean coasts and at inland wetlands, lakes, rivers, and fish-rich waterways. It is generally uncommon to locally fairly common, with notable concentrations in wetland regions such as Río Frío and Caño Negro. It may occasionally be observed at elevations approaching 1,500 m.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, most Ospreys are nonbreeding migrants and winter visitors from North America. Autumn passage is concentrated mainly from September to October, and spring passage from March to April, often following coastal and inland water routes. A small number of individuals may remain during the local summer, but regular breeding in Costa Rica is not established.
value.breeding: Ospreys usually breed near productive water, placing large stick nests on trees, cliffs, utility structures, platforms, or other elevated sites. The nest is often reused and enlarged over many years. A typical clutch contains two to four eggs, and incubation is shared, with the female doing most of it while the male supplies food. Young remain dependent for several weeks after fledging. Birds seen in Costa Rica are generally migrants or nonbreeding visitors rather than members of a resident breeding population.
value.dietFeeding: Fish make up almost the entire diet. The Osprey hunts from perches or while hovering, then plunges feet-first into shallow water to seize prey near the surface. Its long claws, rough foot pads, and reversible outer toe help it grip slippery fish. It commonly carries prey head-first while flying to a perch or nest. Occasionally it takes other aquatic animals, but these are minor components of its diet.
value.behavior: The Osprey is usually seen alone or in pairs, soaring, circling over water, or scanning from exposed perches. It often hovers briefly before diving and may shake water from its feathers after a capture. Individuals defend feeding areas less strongly than many raptors, so several may gather where fish are abundant. During migration, birds can travel along coastlines and through inland corridors. Calls are high-pitched whistles, most often given near nests or during social interactions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable overall, although trends differ among regions. Many populations declined severely during the twentieth century because of persecution and contaminants such as DDT, followed by substantial recovery after protective measures and pesticide restrictions.
